title: The cave (Sn 4.2)
hookLine: read it: a person stuck in the cave of the body
tomorrow: someone praises their own goodness, unasked. what's wrong with that?

lines: A CAVE CLOSER THAN YOUR ROOM.
cards: There's a kind of day that comes now and then. Blanket, phone, snacks, curtains half shut. The hours slide by, and the room gets smaller and cozier and harder to leave.
Nobody locked the door. It just holds you. The second poem of the chapter of eights is about a cave like that, and its readers say the cave is even closer than your room.
It's the body, and the life wrapped around it.

teach.h: STUCK IN THE CAVE, COVERED OVER.
teach.b: Here's the poem from the Sutta Nipata, in plain paraphrase. A person stays in the cave, covered over by many things, sunk in confusion, far from any quiet.

teach.h: NO ONE ELSE CAN FREE THEM.
teach.b: Bound by wishes, tied to the pleasure of being alive, they're hard to free, and the poem says no one else can free them. They lean forward into what's coming and back into what's gone.
And when pain arrives, they ask: what will become of us when we die? So, the poem says, train right here. Don't do what you know is wrong for the sake of any of it.
Life is short, the wise say.
Then the image that stays: people trembling, caught by craving, like fish in a stream that's almost dried up. Seeing that, live without grabbing at mine. Pull out the dart.
Notice how ordinary the cave is. No dragon, no chains. Just layers: comfort, habit, fear, the pull of before and after.
And notice the hard line in the middle. Nobody else opens it. Not a parent, not a teacher, not a good piece of news.
The first step out is seeing the walls as walls.

how: Buddhist students sometimes read a short poem like this one slowly, a verse at a time, and then reflect on what in their own life it describes; the image of fish in a drying stream is a familiar one in teaching on craving.

o: being held in place by wishes, fears and comfort
a quiet place a monk goes to meditate alone
the darkness after death, before rebirth

games.q: inside the cave poem — tap the pairs.
p: read as the body and its life
pulled out by the one who's free

s: the cave in the poem is a meditation cave to retreat into
it's where a person is stuck: covered over by wishes and fears, read as the body.
the poem says no one else can free the person in the cave
bound by wishes, they're hard to free, and not by someone else.
the poem compares people caught by craving to fish in a drying stream
trembling, with the water running out.

games.q: your cousin says she'll start drawing again once her parents stop nagging her about grades. by the poem, who opens the cave?
o: she does: the poem says no one else frees you.
her parents, as soon as they finally ease up.
an art teacher who can pull her out of it.
games.why: the poem's hard line: people bound by wishes are hard to free, and no one else frees them. the nagging may be real; the cave is still hers to see.

practice: Take a pen and write one line by hand: what holds me right now is… and finish it honestly. Don't fix it or judge it.
Set the pen down, keep the line where you can see it, and breathe with it, the way you'd look at a room you're about to step out of.

wordCard.voice: The cave: the poem's picture of a person held in place, covered over by wishes and fears, read as the body and the life around it.

orig.note: Pali: cave, hiding place. The poem is the Guhaṭṭhaka Sutta, the eight verses on the cave.

carryVoice: Here's your line: the cave, warm walls that only you can see for what they are. Poem two, done.
